title: Read the clock
goal: Say one time in official and everyday German.

objectives.title: Ask for and tell the time
Convert official times to halb, Viertel, vor and nach
Clock units and time questions

cards.title: Two ways to read one clock
cards.body: Official time uses the hour, Uhr, then minutes, usually on a 24-hour clock. Everyday time uses twelve hours. Nach means after; vor means before. Halb names the next hour: halb acht is halfway to eight, so it means 7:30.

examples.why: Official time gives sixteen hours and ten minutes.
Nach counts minutes after four; the context supplies morning or afternoon.

cards.title: Aim at the next hour
cards.body: Think of the next hour as a destination. Halb means halfway there; Viertel vor means fifteen minutes before it. Viertel nach counts fifteen minutes after the current hour. Ask Wie spät ist es? Use Es ist for the answer; add um when saying when something happens.

examples.why: The named destination is eleven, so subtract half an hour.

examples.de: Der Film beginnt um Viertel vor neun.
examples.en: The film starts at quarter to nine.
examples.why: Viertel vor neun is 8:45; um introduces the start time.

references.title: Clock conversions
references.note: At a full hour say ein Uhr, but everyday eins without Uhr. Es ist ein Uhr uses ein before Uhr; Es ist eins uses the standalone number. Some regions use viertel acht for 7:15 and dreiviertel acht for 7:45; this course practices Viertel nach/vor.

terms.meaning: halfway to the next named hour
a quarter: fifteen minutes

practice.prompt: Which everyday expression means 18:30?
practice.explanation: Halfway to seven is 6:30; evening context makes it 18:30.

practice.prompt: Build: It is quarter past five.
practice.explanation: Nach counts forward from five.

practice.prompt: Complete with the missing word: Es ist zehn ___ sechs. (5:50)
practice.explanation: Ten minutes before six is ten vor sechs.
practice.hint: halfway to the next named hour

blind.prompt: Write 10:45 as a full sentence with Es ist and Viertel vor; spell out the hour.
blind.explanation: The next hour is eleven; a quarter before it is 10:45.

reading.title: A station clock
reading.text: Anna steht am Bahnhof. Es ist acht Uhr fünfzehn. Ihr Zug kommt um halb neun. Sie hat noch fünfzehn Minuten Zeit. Ben fragt: „Wie spät ist es?“ Anna sagt: „Viertel nach acht.“ Dann kaufen Anna und Ben einen Kaffee.
reading.translation: Anna is at the station. It is 8:15. Her train arrives at half past eight. She still has fifteen minutes. Ben asks, “What time is it?” Anna says, “Quarter past eight.” Then Anna and Ben buy a coffee.

questions.explanation: Halb neun names 8:30.
Her direct answer is Viertel nach acht.
The text says noch fünfzehn Minuten.

listening.title: A cinema announcement
listening.text: Guten Abend! Der Film beginnt heute um neunzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig, also um Viertel vor acht. Es ist jetzt halb acht. Sie haben noch fünfzehn Minuten. Die Kasse ist hier links. Vielen Dank!
listening.translation: Good evening! The film starts today at 19:45, that is, quarter to eight. It is now half past seven. You still have fifteen minutes. The ticket office is here on the left. Thank you!

questions.prompt: What is the official start time?
questions.explanation: Neunzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig is 19:45.
Halb acht is 7:30, here in the evening.
Hier links means here on the left.

writing.prompt: Your friend asks the time. Write one sentence for 6:15 using Es ist and Viertel nach.
writing.explanation: Viertel nach six is fifteen minutes after six.
writing.hint: halfway to the next named hour

title: Plan an ordinary day
goal: Describe a routine with a day, a clock time and a time range.

objectives.title: Use am, um and von … bis
Describe daily routines in sequence
Daily activities and parts of the day

cards.title: Choose the size of the time
cards.body: Use am with a weekday or part of the day, and um with a clock time. Von … bis gives a start and finish. A time phrase can come first; the conjugated verb still occupies the second position, so the person comes after it.

examples.why: Am introduces the day; arbeite stays second.

examples.de: Ich lerne von neun bis elf Uhr.
examples.en: I study from nine to eleven.
examples.why: Von introduces the start and bis the finish.

cards.title: Fill three calendar boxes
cards.body: Imagine a calendar with a day box, a time box and a duration bar. Am fills the day box, um fills the time box, and von … bis fills the bar. Keep the verb next to the first complete phrase. Dann means then and also takes the first position.

examples.why: The whole time phrase fills position one, so frühstückt comes next.

examples.de: Ben duscht am Morgen. Dann arbeitet er.
examples.en: Ben showers in the morning. Then he works.
examples.why: Am Morgen identifies the part of the day; after Dann, arbeitet precedes er.

references.title: Time phrases
rows: am Morgen / am Vormittag / am Mittag / am Nachmittag / am Abend
references.note: Am Abend lerne ich names an evening period; Ich schlafe in der Nacht uses the fixed night expression. Morgens arbeite ich means mornings in general; Am Morgen arbeite ich can describe one morning. Dann koche ich means then I cook, with verb second.

terms.meaning: am for a day or day part; um for a clock time
from a start until a finish

watch: Say Am Montag arbeite ich, with arbeite before ich after the time phrase.

practice.prompt: Choose the pair: ___ Freitag ___ 15 Uhr.
practice.explanation: Friday is a day; 15 Uhr is a clock time.

practice.prompt: Build: On Monday I study.
practice.explanation: The day phrase occupies the first position.

practice.prompt: Complete: Ich arbeite von acht ___ zwölf Uhr.
practice.explanation: The pair is von … bis.
practice.hint: am for a day or day part; um for a clock time

blind.prompt: Say 'I work from ten to twelve o'clock.' Start Ich and spell out the times.
answers: Ich arbeite von zehn bis zwölf Uhr.
blind.explanation: Von and bis frame the time range.

retrieval.prompt: Say 'I shower in the morning.' Start Ich.
Say 'On Thursday I study.' Start Am.
Say 'Then I eat.' Start Dann.

reading.title: A library day
reading.text: Leon lernt am Mittwoch in der Bibliothek. Um acht Uhr frühstückt er. Von neun bis zwölf Uhr liest er. Am Mittag isst er eine Suppe. Dann arbeitet er von dreizehn bis sechzehn Uhr. Am Abend besucht er Anna.
reading.translation: Leon studies at the library on Wednesday. He has breakfast at eight. He reads from nine to twelve. At midday he eats a soup. Then he works from thirteen to sixteen. In the evening he visits Anna.

questions.explanation: Am Mittwoch identifies Wednesday.
Von neun bis zwölf Uhr reads 9–12.
Am Abend besucht er Anna gives the evening action.

listening.title: An afternoon plan
listening.text: Mira: Wann arbeitest du morgen, Ben? Ben: Von acht bis vierzehn Uhr. Dann habe ich Zeit. Mira: Gut. Wir lernen am Nachmittag, um drei Uhr. Ben: Ja, und am Abend koche ich. Kommst du auch?
listening.translation: Mira: When do you work tomorrow, Ben? Ben: From eight to fourteen. Then I have time. Mira: Good. We study in the afternoon, at three. Ben: Yes, and in the evening I cook. Are you coming too?

questions.explanation: Bis vierzehn Uhr is the end.
Am Nachmittag makes drei Uhr 15:00.

questions.prompt: What does Ben do in the evening?
questions.explanation: Am Abend koche ich gives his plan.

writing.prompt: Write two sentences: You have breakfast at seven and work from eight to twelve. Start each with Ich. Spell out the times.
answers: Ich frühstücke um sieben Uhr. Ich arbeite von acht bis zwölf Uhr.
Um sieben Uhr frühstücke ich. Von acht bis zwölf Uhr arbeite ich.
writing.explanation: Um gives a point in time; von … bis gives a range.
writing.model: Ich frühstücke um sieben Uhr. Ich arbeite von acht bis zwölf Uhr.
writing.hint: am for a day or day part; um for a clock time

title: Introduce your family
goal: Say who family members are and whom you visit.

objectives.title: Use every possessive article in nominative and accusative
Family relationships
Distinguish consonant r and vowel-like final r

cards.title: The owner and the noun
cards.body: A possessive article means my, your or their. Choose its stem from the owner, then its ending from the noun. Nominative identifies the subject or follows Das ist. Accusative marks a direct object after besuchen or sehen. Only masculine singular adds -en in this contrast.

examples.why: Mein agrees with masculine Bruder as the subject.
Bruder is now the masculine direct object, so mein becomes meinen.

cards.title: Ask two separate questions
cards.body: First ask who owns or belongs with someone: I gives mein, she gives ihr. Then ask what follows: a masculine object needs -en; feminine and plural use -e; neuter stays unextended. In Schwester and Vater, final -er often sounds like a short unstressed 'a'; the r in Bruder before a vowel is consonantal.

examples.why: The owner is she, giving ihr; feminine Tochter gives ihre.
Wir gives unser, and neuter accusative Kind adds no ending.

references.title: Possessives: nominative
references.note: Mein Vater ist hier uses nominative because Vater is the subject. Meine Eltern sind hier uses -e because Eltern is plural. Euer loses an e before endings: eure Mutter.

references.title: Possessives: accusative
references.note: Ich sehe euren Vater uses euren because Vater is masculine and seen. Ich sehe eure Mutter uses eure because Mutter is feminine. Capital Ihr/Ihre/Ihren addresses someone formally; lower-case ihr can mean her or their.

references.title: Family and r sounds
rows: father / mother: unstressed final -er is vowel-like
husband / wife in a family context
r after a long vowel or final -er often becomes vowel-like
references.note: Hear the difference in Bruder and Vater: Bruder has r starting a syllable, while Vater ends in weak -er. Say hören with an r before the next vowel; say Uhr without forcing an English r. Regional r sounds vary.

terms.meaning: a word before a noun showing whose person or thing it is
the direct-object form, often after seeing or visiting

watch: His daughter is seine Tochter: the owner chooses sein, but the daughter chooses -e.

practice.explanation: Vater is a masculine accusative object.

practice.prompt: Build: Our daughter is called Anna.

practice.explanation: Ihr as the owner gives euer; before -e it becomes eure.

blind.explanation: Her gives ihr; masculine accusative Bruder needs ihren.

reading.title: A family message
reading.text: Meine Familie wohnt in Bonn. Mein Vater heißt Ben und meine Mutter heißt Anna. Unser Haus ist klein. Meine Schwester Mira besucht heute unsere Oma. Ich sehe meinen Bruder am Sonntag. Unsere Eltern kochen dann, und wir essen zusammen.
reading.translation: My family lives in Bonn. My father is called Ben and my mother is called Anna. Our house is small. My sister Mira visits our grandma today. I see my brother on Sunday. Our parents then cook, and we eat together.

questions.explanation: Meine Schwester Mira besucht heute unsere Oma.

questions.prompt: When does the writer see the brother?
questions.explanation: Am Sonntag is the stated day.
Unsere Eltern kochen identifies the cooks.

listening.title: A photo conversation
listening.text: Leon: Ist das dein Bruder? Mira: Nein, das ist mein Cousin Ben. Mein Bruder heißt Paul. Leon: Und die Frau hier? Mira: Das ist unsere Tante. Wir besuchen unseren Onkel und unsere Tante am Samstag. Kommst du mit?
listening.translation: Leon: Is that your brother? Mira: No, that is my cousin Ben. My brother is called Paul. Leon: And the woman here? Mira: That is our aunt. We visit our uncle and our aunt on Saturday. Are you coming along?

questions.explanation: Das ist mein Cousin Ben corrects Leon.
Das ist unsere Tante identifies her.
Am Samstag gives the visit day.

writing.prompt: Write two sentences: Your brother is called Leon. You visit your brother today. Use mein/meinen and start Mein, then Ich.
answers: Mein Bruder heißt Leon. Ich besuche meinen Bruder heute.
Mein Bruder heißt Leon. Heute besuche ich meinen Bruder.
writing.explanation: The subject uses mein; the visited masculine object uses meinen.
writing.model: Mein Bruder heißt Leon. Ich besuche meinen Bruder heute.
writing.hint: a word before a noun showing whose person or thing it is

title: Can, must and want
goal: Explain availability using müssen, können and wollen.

objectives.title: Conjugate müssen, können and wollen for all persons
Build modal brackets in statements and questions
Accept or decline a plan with a reason

cards.title: Two verbs make a frame
cards.body: A modal verb adds must, can or want to an action. Conjugate the modal for the person, but leave the action in its dictionary form, called the infinitive. In a statement the modal is second and the infinitive goes last. A yes/no question starts with the modal.

examples.why: Muss is the conjugated modal; arbeiten closes the sentence.
The question starts with kannst and ends with kommen.

cards.title: Keep the action at the far end
cards.body: Think of a modal as opening a frame and the action as closing it. Put the person, time and other details between them. Können can express ability or availability; müssen expresses necessity; wollen expresses an intention or strong wish, so it can sound direct in requests.

examples.en: We want to visit our grandma.
examples.why: Wollen matches wir; besuchen remains an infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Am Dienstag kann Mira nicht kommen.
examples.why: The time comes first, kann stays second, and kommen stays last.

references.title: Complete modal forms
references.note: Ich and er/es/sie share a form without -t: er kann, not er kannt. Du musst gehen uses musst for du and gehen last. Ihr wollt lernen uses wollt for ihr and lernen last.

references.title: Modal frame
references.note: Wir können schwimmen describes ability; Wir können am Montag kommen describes availability. Ich will einen Termin sounds direct; Ich möchte einen Termin is a gentler request learned as a polite phrase.

terms.meaning: a verb adding ability, necessity or intention to an action
the dictionary form of the action, placed last after a modal

watch: Do not conjugate the final action: Ich kann kommen, not Ich kann komme.

practice.prompt: Choose the correct modal sentence.
practice.explanation: Er takes muss; the final action stays arbeiten.

practice.prompt: Build: We want to cook today.
practice.explanation: The modal opens and the infinitive closes the frame.

practice.prompt: Complete: Ihr ___ am Samstag kommen. (can)
practice.explanation: The ihr form of können is könnt.
practice.hint: a verb adding ability, necessity or intention to an action

blind.explanation: After Morgen, muss is second and lernen last.

retrieval.prompt: Ask 'Can you come?' Use informal singular.
Translate 'She wants to cook.' Start Sie.
Translate 'We cannot work today.' Start Wir.
retrieval.explanation: Können agrees with wir; arbeiten closes the frame.

reading.title: Too many plans
reading.text: Ben will am Samstag Fußball spielen. Er muss aber am Vormittag arbeiten. Seine Schwester kann erst am Nachmittag kommen. Die beiden wollen dann ihre Eltern besuchen. Am Abend können sie zusammen kochen. Ben sagt: „Gut, ich muss heute noch einkaufen.“
reading.translation: Ben wants to play football on Saturday. But he must work in the morning. His sister can only come in the afternoon. The two then want to visit their parents. In the evening they can cook together. Ben says, “Good, I must still shop today.”

questions.prompt: Why is Ben busy in the morning?
questions.explanation: Er muss … am Vormittag arbeiten gives the necessity.
Erst am Nachmittag states her earliest availability.

questions.prompt: What do they want to do together?
questions.explanation: Die beiden wollen … ihre Eltern besuchen.

listening.title: Arrange a game
listening.text: Anna: Wollt ihr heute Tennis spielen? Leon: Ich kann nicht. Ich muss bis sechs Uhr lernen. Anna: Und morgen? Leon: Morgen können wir spielen. Ben will auch kommen. Anna: Gut, dann wollen wir um fünf Uhr anfangen.
listening.translation: Anna: Do you want to play tennis today? Leon: I can't. I must study until six. Anna: And tomorrow? Leon: Tomorrow we can play. Ben wants to come too. Anna: Good, then we want to start at five.

questions.prompt: Why can Leon not play today?
questions.explanation: Ich muss … lernen gives his reason.
Ben will auch kommen.
Um fünf Uhr is the proposed start.

answers: Ich muss heute arbeiten. Ich kann morgen kommen.
Heute muss ich arbeiten. Morgen kann ich kommen.
writing.explanation: Muss and kann match ich; each final action remains infinitive.
writing.model: Ich muss heute arbeiten. Ich kann morgen kommen.

title: Make a phone appointment
goal: Prepare and complete a short appointment call.

objectives.title: Request, negotiate and confirm an appointment by phone
Prepare a call with notes and repeat key details
Appointment and phone phrases

cards.title: Prepare three small notes
cards.body: Before calling, write your name, the reason for the call and two possible times. Have a calendar and pen ready. Ich hätte gern is a fixed polite phrase meaning I would like. Offer or reject a time, then repeat the agreed day and hour to check understanding.

examples.de: Guten Tag, hier ist Mira. Ich hätte gern einen Termin.
examples.en: Hello, this is Mira. I would like an appointment.
examples.why: The greeting, name and polite request establish the purpose.

examples.de: Geht es am Mittwoch um zehn Uhr?
examples.why: Am gives the day and um gives the clock time.

cards.title: Use a short call route
cards.body: Follow a route: greet, request, choose, confirm, close. If a time fails, say Das geht leider nicht and suggest another. You can ask for repetition instead of guessing. Repeat the final time as a question, then say Auf Wiederhören when ending a phone conversation.

examples.why: The modal können makes a polite request; wiederholen stays last.

examples.de: Also am Freitag um elf Uhr? Vielen Dank. Auf Wiederhören.
examples.en: So Friday at eleven? Thank you. Goodbye.
examples.why: Repeating both day and time checks the appointment; Auf Wiederhören closes a call.

references.title: A complete call toolkit
rows: Können Sie am Montag um neun Uhr kommen?
Wie bitte? Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?
Also am Dienstag um zehn Uhr?

goodbye at the end of a phone call

watch: Do not end a phone call with Auf Wiedersehen when you cannot see each other; use Auf Wiederhören.

title: Explain a delay
goal: Apologize for a delay and give an arrival time.

objectives.title: Apologize for lateness and respond
Compare punctuality expectations in different situations
Delay, apology and arrival phrases

cards.title: Apology plus useful detail
cards.body: An apology acknowledges a delay: Es tut mir leid means I am sorry. Add Ich bin zu spät for arriving late, or Ich komme … Minuten später for an expected delay. Give a new arrival time if possible. The other person can accept with Kein Problem or Macht nichts.

examples.de: Es tut mir leid. Ich bin zu spät.
examples.en: I am sorry. I am late.
examples.why: The first sentence apologizes; the second names the problem.

examples.en: I will arrive ten minutes later.
examples.why: A number plus Minuten später gives the delay clearly.

cards.title: Match the situation
cards.body: A medical appointment, a work meeting and a relaxed café visit may have different expectations. Ask or tell people when you are delayed; avoid assuming one rule fits everyone. A short message works well: apology, delay, revised time. Respond with reassurance or a request to be punctual next time.

examples.de: Entschuldigung, ich komme um halb sechs.
examples.en: Sorry, I will arrive at half past five.
examples.why: The apology is followed by a clear revised clock time.

examples.de: Kein Problem. Das nächste Mal bitte pünktlich.
examples.en: No problem. Next time please be punctual.
examples.why: The response accepts the apology and adds an expectation for next time.

references.title: Delay and response phrases
rows: I will arrive five minutes later.

No problem. / Never mind. / It's all right.

title: Give a date and birthday

cards.title: A date counts position
cards.body: An ordinal is a number showing position: first, second, third. After am, dates usually end in -ten from 1–19 and -sten from 20 onward. Memorize ersten, dritten, siebten and achten. Say the day before the month. A written dot marks an ordinal: 3. means third.

examples.de: Ich habe am dritten Mai Geburtstag.
examples.why: Drei changes to dritten after am.

examples.de: Die Party ist am zwanzigsten Juni.
examples.why: Twenty starts the -sten group.

cards.title: Read a calendar aloud
cards.body: Read 7.8. as am siebten August, or am siebten Achten when both numbers are spoken as ordinals. Month names stay unchanged. Ask Wann hast du Geburtstag? For today’s date use Heute ist der dritte Mai. Hear ei as English eye, eu as oy, and au as ow in now.

examples.why: Acht takes only -en: achten, not achtten.
After der use erste; after am use ersten. Ei in erste is not an ei pair; compare drei, neun and auch for eye, oy and ow.

references.title: Every day of a month after am
references.note: The whole ordinal takes its ending: am einundzwanzigsten Mai means 21 May. Am einunddreißigsten Juli means 31 July. Today’s date uses der: Heute ist der siebte Mai; after am it becomes am siebten Mai.

references.title: Months in calendar order
references.note: A named month does not get an ordinal ending: am zweiten März uses März unchanged. With a numbered month, 2.3. can be am zweiten Dritten: both numbers are ordinals.

references.title: Three moving vowel sounds
references.note: Say drei with one moving vowel sound, not separate e and i. Say Freunde with oy; say Haus with ow. Keep the two letters together as one syllable sound.

cards.title: The prefix moves to the end
cards.body: A separable verb has a small beginning called a prefix. In a normal present sentence, conjugate the main part and send the prefix to the end: einladen becomes lade ... ein. In yes/no questions the conjugated part comes first. With a modal, the whole infinitive stays together at the end.

cards.title: Replace the person receiving the action
cards.body: A pronoun replaces a noun or name. A subject does the action; a direct object receives it. German changes ich to mich, du to dich and er to ihn for the direct object. Use these forms after sehen, abholen and einladen. Es and sie keep their spelling.

cards.title: Für always chooses the object form
cards.body: Für means for. It requires accusative even when the rest of the sentence has no direct object. Ask Für wen? for a person. Masculine der/ein becomes den/einen; feminine die/eine and neuter das/ein stay the same. Use für mich when ordering for yourself and für Sie in formal service.

references.title: Für with nouns

title: Order and pay in a café

cards.title: Use a small order pattern
cards.body: A server may ask Was möchten Sie? Use Ich nehme or Ich hätte gern followed by your order; hätte gern is a polite fixed phrase. The item is an accusative object: einen Kaffee, eine Suppe, ein Wasser. Add bitte. Für mich bitte ... is another polite way to order.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern einen Apfelsaft, bitte.

examples.why: Apfelsaft is masculine, so its object article is einen.

cards.title: Make the payment clear
cards.body: Ask Kann ich bitte zahlen? A server may ask Zusammen oder getrennt? Zusammen means one combined bill; getrennt means each person pays separately. When giving cash, Stimmt so means keep the change. To choose a total including a tip, say Machen Sie ... Euro, bitte. Tipping is a choice, not a fixed lesson requirement.

title: Say how an event was

cards.title: Two useful past verbs
cards.body: The simple past talks about an earlier time. For sein, use war to say what something was like or where someone was. For haben, use hatte for something someone had. These are complete conjugated verbs: no extra infinitive is needed. Add gestern to make the earlier time clear.

cards.title: Ask, then choose was or had
cards.body: Use Wie war ...? to ask for an evaluation. Choose sein for a place, identity or description; choose haben for hunger, thirst, time or fun. Match the ending to the subject: du warst, ihr wart, du hattest, ihr hattet. Keep these verbs second in statements and first in yes/no questions.

title: Reply to a formal letter

cards.title: Find the purpose before you write
cards.body: Identify who sent the letter, why they wrote and what reply they need. The Betreff is the subject line. Address a woman formally with Sehr geehrte Frau plus surname and a man with Sehr geehrter Herr plus surname. Place a comma after the greeting.

examples.de: Sehr geehrte Frau Wolf, vielen Dank für Ihre Einladung.
examples.en: Dear Ms Wolf, thank you for your invitation.
examples.why: Ihre refers politely to the recipient; vielen begins with a small letter after the comma.

examples.de: Sehr geehrter Herr Klein, ich komme gern am Freitag.
examples.en: Dear Mr Klein, I would be happy to come on Friday.
examples.why: Sehr geehrter matches Herr, and the reply confirms the proposed day.

cards.title: Keep the greeting and ending consistent
cards.body: A formal letter closes with Mit freundlichen Grüßen and your signature, with no comma after the closing. A friend can receive Liebe or Lieber plus first name and Viele Grüße. In your reply confirm or decline the requested time and include any question.

examples.de: Liebe Mia, leider habe ich am Dienstag keine Zeit.
examples.en: Dear Mia, unfortunately I have no time on Tuesday.
examples.why: First names allow Liebe and a friendly explanation.
Put the name on a new line. The slash shows a line break and is not part of the letter.

title: Keep a break-time conversation going
goal: Open, respond to and close a short workplace conversation.

cards.title: Start with a shared topic
cards.body: People who hardly know each other can talk about the weather, a weekend plan or sport. Ask a short question, listen and return a question. Match the colleague’s du or Sie. Leave private topics such as pay for a relationship where they are welcome.

examples.de: Wie war Ihr Wochenende? – Sehr schön. Und Ihres?
examples.en: How was your weekend? – Very nice. And yours?
examples.why: Ihr and Ihres keep the exchange formal and the return question includes the listener.

examples.de: Mögen Sie Sport? – Ja, ich schwimme gern.
examples.en: Do you like sport? – Yes, I enjoy swimming.
examples.why: Ja confirms a positive question; the hobby gives a natural follow-up.

cards.title: Check whether the question was negative
cards.body: After a positive question ja confirms and nein denies. After a negative question doch contradicts the negative. Nein agrees that the negative statement is true. Add a sentence after the one-word answer so your colleague knows exactly what you mean.

examples.de: Kommst du nicht mit? – Doch, ich komme mit.
examples.en: Aren’t you coming along? – Yes, I am coming.
examples.why: Doch corrects the assumption that you will stay behind.

examples.de: Trinken Sie keinen Kaffee? – Nein, ich trinke Tee.
examples.en: Don’t you drink coffee? – No, I drink tea.
examples.why: Nein confirms the negative. The next sentence removes doubt.
